texts.title: How a city measures its air

paragraphs.text: Air pollution is invisible on most days and is measured anyway, because the effects are cumulative and the sources are numerous. A city that wants to act has first to know what is in its air, where it comes from and when, and each of those three questions is answered by a different kind of instrument. The public argument is usually about limits; the technical argument, which decides what actually happens, is about measurement. A limit that cannot be measured reliably is a limit that will be argued about rather than met.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The reference instruments are few, expensive and slow. A regulatory monitoring station costs as much as a house, sits in a small building with a climate-controlled interior, and produces data that a court will accept; a city of a million people may have five or six. They are sited according to rules that try to represent typical exposure rather than the worst corner, which is why a resident can stand in obvious traffic fumes and be told that the official reading is acceptable, and be correct in the objection. The station is not lying; it is answering a different question from the one the resident is asking.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Low-cost sensors filled the gap and brought their own problems. A device the size of a book can be hung on a lamp post for the price of a meal, and a network of hundreds gives a picture of how pollution moves through a city that no reference station can. What such a sensor measures, however, drifts with humidity, temperature and age, and two identical units can disagree substantially after a wet month. Used without correction against a reference instrument, they produce maps that are confidently wrong. A confident wrong map is worse than none, because somebody will plan a school run around it.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Correcting them is now a routine discipline. A sensor placed beside a reference station for a few weeks yields a relationship that can be applied to its later readings, and the relationship is rechecked periodically because it changes. Networks that do this produce data good enough for planning; networks that do not produce data good enough for headlines. The difference is invisible in the published map and obvious in the documentation, which is one reason the documentation is worth reading.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Knowing where the pollution comes from requires something else again. Chemical fingerprinting identifies sources by the ratio of substances in a sample: traffic, wood burning, industry and construction each leave a different signature, and the proportions can be estimated for a given district. The results regularly surprise the authorities that commission them, with domestic wood burning turning out to be a larger contributor in several cities than the traffic that dominates the political discussion.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The time pattern matters as much as the total and is often ignored. Exposure that occurs while people are asleep indoors is less harmful than the same concentration at the school gate at nine in the morning, and a limit expressed as an annual average can be met by a city in which the worst hours are very bad indeed. Several authorities now publish hourly data and set targets on peaks, which is harder to meet and closer to what the health evidence describes.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Measurement changes behaviour in ways that are not always the intended ones. A street with a public display of its readings sees fewer idling engines; a school with its own sensor produces parents who ask questions at meetings; and a city whose figures are about to breach a limit sometimes finds reasons to move a monitoring station, which has happened often enough to be studied. The instrument is never neutral once somebody is judged by it.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What the field agrees on is that measurement is necessary and is not the point. The purpose is to decide where to put a low-traffic zone, which boilers to replace, when to close a road to lorries and whether last year’s scheme worked, and a city that measures beautifully and acts on none of it has bought an expensive thermometer. Several cities have done exactly that, published a handsome dashboard and changed nothing on any street. The measurement, in other words, is the beginning of the argument rather than the end of it.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: The trade that moved the world

paragraphs.text: Spices are a strange thing to have reorganised the world. They are not food, they do not preserve anything as well as salt, and the quantities involved were tiny; a ship that carried a hundred tonnes of pepper was carrying a fortune in a volume that would fill a modern lorry. What made them valuable was that they grew in a few specific places, kept well on a long journey, and were wanted by people who could pay. Value per kilogram is the quality that makes a long sea route worth sailing, and it is the reason this particular cargo shaped the map.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The trade is far older than the European voyages that are usually credited with it. Cloves from a handful of islands have been found in kitchens thousands of kilometres away, in deposits dating from long before any recorded contact between the two regions, and the routes that carried them were established by traders who left no written account. Most of the history of this commerce belongs to people whose names are unknown. The written record begins where the Europeans arrive, which is a fact about the record rather than about the trade.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The prices along the route did the most to shape events. A spice that cost little at its source passed through a chain of intermediaries, each adding a margin, and arrived at the far end of the chain at a multiple that is startling to read about. That multiple was an invitation to anybody who could shorten the chain, and the search for a direct route is the motive behind a long series of voyages that are usually described in other terms.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Control of the source was the prize and turned out to be the trap. Powers that reached the growing regions tried to hold a monopoly by controlling the islands, destroying plantations elsewhere and executing those who traded outside the system; the effort consumed ships, soldiers and money on a scale that the profits eventually could not justify. A monopoly on a plant is only as good as the difficulty of growing the plant somewhere else, and nobody involved seems to have asked how difficult that actually was.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Somewhere else arrived in the eighteenth century and ended the arrangement. Seedlings were smuggled out, planted in other tropical territories, and grew perfectly well; within a few decades the price fell to a level at which the monopoly was worthless, and a commodity that had justified wars became an item in an ordinary cargo. The fall is one of the clearest examples of what happens to a rent that depends on a barrier when the barrier is removed. Nothing about the plant changed; what changed was that it now grew in more than one place.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The effects on the places that grew the spices outlasted the trade. Populations were moved, replaced or destroyed; land was converted to a single crop and the food systems that had supported the islands were not rebuilt when the price collapsed; and the political boundaries drawn by trading companies survive as the borders of states. The history is remembered very differently at the two ends of the route, which is ordinary and is worth stating plainly.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: What the spices did to European food is smaller than the drama suggests. Heavily spiced cooking was a fashion of the wealthy and faded as the prices fell, which is the reverse of what one would expect: the cuisines that use the most spice today are those of the regions where the spices grow, and the cooking of the countries that fought over them is comparatively plain. Scarcity, not taste, was doing the work.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The pattern is worth recognising because it recurs. A commodity is valuable because of where it grows, a chain of intermediaries captures most of the value, somebody tries to control the source by force, the crop is moved, the price collapses, and the places that grew it are left with an economy built for a market that has gone. Substitute a mineral or a fuel for the spice and the account describes several more recent episodes without changing a word. That is the reason the story is taught in economics as often as in history.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: A zoo is an institution with four purposes and a single gate. It entertains, it educates, it conducts research and it breeds animals whose wild populations are in trouble, and the four sit together uneasily because the animals that draw a crowd are not always the ones that need the help. The argument about whether zoos should exist is usually conducted as though the answer were the same for all of them, which is the first thing wrong with it.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Helena Marsh defends the conservation case with numbers rather than sentiment. Several species exist only because a captive population was maintained while the causes of their decline were addressed, and a handful have been returned to the wild in numbers that now sustain themselves; the programmes that achieved this required decades, international coordination and a genetic register of every individual. She is careful to add that this describes a small number of species and cannot be claimed for a collection as a whole.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Kwame Osei doubts that the conservation argument justifies the institution. Most of the animals in most zoos belong to species that are not endangered, are not part of any breeding programme and will never be released, he argues, and their presence is explained by visitor numbers rather than by biology. He accepts that the money from those visitors funds the serious work, and asks whether a funding model that requires a popular exhibit is a good way to pay for conservation.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Yuki Tanabe works on what captivity does to the animals themselves. Enclosures have improved beyond recognition, and the measurable welfare of most species in a well-run modern zoo is better than the older literature would suggest; the exceptions are consistent and are the animals that range widely, the great predators and the largest of the social mammals, for which no enclosure that can be built resembles the life the animal is adapted to. Her position is not that zoos are cruel but that some species should not be in them.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Marta Reyes studies whether visitors learn anything. Surveys taken at the exit show enthusiasm and little retained information, and studies that follow visitors afterwards find small effects on knowledge and almost none on behaviour; the exception is a visit that includes a structured programme with a person explaining, which produces measurable learning and is expensive per head. Her conclusion is that a zoo which claims education as a purpose should be judged on what it can demonstrate rather than on attendance.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The alternatives that are usually proposed turn out to be narrower than they sound. A reserve in the country of origin protects animals in their habitat and depends on the stability of that country and on funding from elsewhere; a sanctuary takes animals that cannot be released and does not breed them; a film shows an animal to millions and puts nothing into the field. None of these replaces the others, and the useful question is what each is good for rather than which should win.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Regulation has already answered part of the argument. Standards for space, enrichment and veterinary care are legal requirements in many countries, several species are no longer kept because the standards cannot be met in practice, and collections that fail inspection close. This is a slower and less satisfying process than a general ban and it has removed most of the institutions that the general argument is really about.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The defensible position is therefore specific. A collection is worth having if the species it keeps are chosen for a reason it can state, if the animals that cannot be housed properly are not there, if the education programme is measured, and if the research and breeding work is real rather than decorative. That standard would close a number of zoos and leave others stronger, which is a duller outcome than either side of the argument wants and is the one the evidence supports. It also has the advantage of being a standard a collection can be measured against, rather than a position it can announce, and the difference between those two things is most of what the argument has been missing. A visitor can apply it too, in about ten minutes, by reading the signs and asking what the collection says it is for.
paragraphs.label: H
